subject: TrueCap #9 — Section 8 rentals: the honest math
preheader: Voucher rents +12% above market in some zones · The screening trade-off · 3 deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Quiet summer week — but voucher market is moving
marketSnapshot.body: Rates flat at 6.64%. The interesting movement this week isn't in rates — it's in HUD Fair Market Rent updates published last Thursday for federal fiscal year 2027. FMRs are up 4-9% in most of our covered Midwest markets, which means Section 8 voucher rents in those zones are now meaningfully above market rent on B/C-class properties. If you've avoided Section 8 because of stereotypes about tenant quality or paperwork, the new FMR makes the math harder to ignore.

dealSpotter.body: $105k purchase, comparable rental at $1,275. Section 8 FMR for a 3-bedroom in this zone is $1,485 (16% premium). Even after accounting for the inspection requirements, the longer screening process, and the occasional damaged-unit headaches you hear about, that 16% rent premium absorbs a lot of friction. The math also benefits from guaranteed payment from the housing authority (the voucher portion arrives like clockwork; you only collect a small tenant portion privately).

$165k 2-unit. Both units would qualify for the local FMR which pays $985 and $1,095. Market rents in the neighborhood are $850-$925. The compounding effect over a 10-year hold of that ~$200/month rent gap is roughly $24k of additional NOI per unit, which gets capitalized into the exit value — not a small effect.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Market rent close to FMR · regular rental wins
dealSpotter.body: $185k 3/1.5. Market rent here is $1,650, voucher FMR is $1,680 — barely a premium. In zones where the market has caught up to FMR, the friction of accepting vouchers (annual inspection, longer turnover, the political risk that voucher programs face) probably isn't worth a 1-2% rent bump. Run the screening cost-benefit per zone, not on aspirational averages.

blogFeature.title: The 50% rule for rentals — still useful in 2026?
blogFeature.excerpt: The old rule says expenses run 50% of gross rent. It's a rough triage tool — useful for the back of a napkin, dangerous if you use it instead of a real underwrite. The cases where it's accurate, the cases where it's off by 15+ points, and how to know which you're in.

qa.question: Section 8 keeps coming up in conversations. Am I avoiding it for good reasons or just lazy bias?
qa.answer: Probably some of both. The 'good reasons' to be cautious: tenant screening on a Section 8 lease is more constrained (you can't reject for some of the same reasons you'd reject a market-rate tenant), the unit must pass annual housing-quality inspections (which can require small remediation work each year), and there's a longer initial lease-up period because the housing authority processes paperwork. The 'lazy bias' to set aside: voucher tenants are not statistically worse renters than the bottom 30% of market-rate tenants in the same price band. The screening + payment-guarantee combo often produces better outcomes than chasing the cheapest market-rate applicant. If you've never tried it on one unit, it's worth running the experiment with a single property before forming a permanent opinion.
